# Kaplan-Meier survival

This is a simple function to estimate Kaplan-Meier survival.

```{r}
#' Kaplan-Meier survival
#' @param time what?
#' @param status what?
#' @return what?
#' @examples
#' time <- c(2, 3, 5, 6, 8)
#' status <- c(1, 1, 0, 1, 0)
#' km(time, status)
#' survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1) |> summary()
km <- function(time, status) {
  ts <- sort(unique(time[status == 1]))
  S <- 1
  out <- data.frame(time = ts, n = NA, d = NA, S = NA)
  for (i in seq_along(ts)) {
    t <- ts[i]
    n <- sum(time >= t)
    d <- sum(time == t & status == 1)
    S <- S * (1 - d / n)
    out$n[i] <- n
    out$d[i] <- d
    out$S[i] <- S
  }
  out
}

# Vectorised version
km2 <- function(time, status) {
  t <- sort(unique(time[status == 1]))
  n <- sapply(t, function(z) sum(time >= z))
  d <- sapply(t, function(z) sum(time == z & status == 1))
  data.frame(time = t, n, d, S = cumprod(1 - d / n))
}
```

**1.** Run the example (see `@examples` above) to verify similarity between `km()`, `km2()` and the survival package equivalent. Are there any differences?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** The example is run below: `km()` and `km2()` return identical tables, and
`summary(survfit(...))` gives the same $\hat S(t)$ at the three event times, plus standard
errors and confidence intervals. So the point estimates agree; the only difference is that
`survfit` additionally reports standard errors and confidence intervals (and marks the
censored observations at times 5 and 8).

```{r}
time <- c(2, 3, 5, 6, 8)
status <- c(1, 1, 0, 1, 0)

km(time, status)
km2(time, status)
summary(survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1))
```
:::

Include the function definition above (copy and paste either `km()` or `km2()` into a code block in your report) and:

**2.** Replace "what?" in the function description with relevant information

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** The `roxygen`-style description should document the arguments and the
return value:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#' Kaplan-Meier survival
#' @param time   numeric vector of observed (follow-up) times; censored times included.
#' @param status event indicator of the same length as `time`: 1 = event, 0 = right-censored.
#' @return a data.frame with one row per distinct event time and columns `time` (event
#'   time), `n` (number at risk just before the event), `d` (number of events) and `S`
#'   (the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the survivor function).
```
:::

**3.** Add detailed comments within the function to explain what it does (step by step)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** The function walks through the distinct event times in order. At each event
time it counts how many subjects are still at risk (`n`) and how many die (`d`), then
updates the estimate by the conditional survival fraction $(n - d)/n$. The product of these
terms over the event times is the Kaplan-Meier (product-limit) estimator.

```{r}
#| eval: false
km <- function(time, status) {
  # Only event times cause a drop; censored times reduce the risk set but no one
  # dies at them, so the estimate is flat there.
  ts <- sort(unique(time[status == 1]))
  S <- 1 # start at S(0) = 1
  out <- data.frame(time = ts, n = NA, d = NA, S = NA)
  for (i in seq_along(ts)) {
    t <- ts[i]
    n <- sum(time >= t) # risk set: subjects still under observation at t
    d <- sum(time == t & status == 1) # events at exactly time t
    S <- S * (1 - d / n) # product-limit: multiply (n - d)/n
    out$n[i] <- n
    out$d[i] <- d
    out$S[i] <- S
  }
  out
}
```
:::

**4.** Modify the function to add 95 % confidence intervals to the point estimates. HINT: eq 2.11/2.12 in Collett, `?cumsum` and Wald CI.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** Equation 2.11 is Greenwood's formula for the variance of $\hat S(t)$:

$$\operatorname{Var}\{\hat S(t)\} \approx \hat S(t)^2 \sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{n_j (n_j - d_j)}.$$

The sum is accumulated over event times with `cumsum`, the standard error is its square
root, and the Wald 95% interval is $\hat S(t) \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}\{\hat S(t)\}$. The
function below implements this and is then called on the example data:

```{r}
km_ci <- function(time, status) {
  t <- sort(unique(time[status == 1]))
  n <- sapply(t, function(z) sum(time >= z))
  d <- sapply(t, function(z) sum(time == z & status == 1))
  S <- cumprod(1 - d / n)
  var_S <- S^2 * cumsum(d / (n * (n - d))) # Greenwood (eq 2.12)
  se <- sqrt(var_S)
  data.frame(
    time = t,
    n,
    d,
    S = S,
    SE = se,
    lower = S - 1.96 * se,
    upper = S + 1.96 * se
  )
}

knitr::kable(km_ci(time, status), digits = 3)
```

Note that the Wald interval lies outside $[0,1]$ (the lower bound at time 6 is negative
and the upper bound at time 2 exceeds 1). This is why `survfit` uses a log-transformed
interval by default (see question 5).
:::

**5.** Again, compare the results between `km()` (or `km2()`) and the survival package equivalent. Are they the same? If not, why? HINT: check argument `conf.type` in `?survfit.formula` (can you reproduce your results by changing this argument?).

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** The point estimates $\hat S(t)$ and the standard errors agree with
`survfit` - both use Greenwood's formula. The *confidence interval bounds* do **not**
match `survfit`'s default output, because `survfit` applies a log transformation
(`conf.type = "log"`, the default) before forming the interval, which forces the interval
inside $[0,1]$. To reproduce the Wald interval more closely, use `conf.type = "plain"`:

```{r}
summary(survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, conf.type = "plain"))
```
:::

**Bonus:** Re-define: `time <- c(2, 2, 1, 3, 2)` and `status <- c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0)` and rerun the analysis. What happened to the SE/CI? Why?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** With the new data the event times are 1, 2 and 3. At the last event time,
$t = 3$, the single subject still at risk dies, so $n_3 = d_3 = 1$ and $n_3 - d_3 = 0$.
Greenwood's term $d_j/(n_j(n_j-d_j)) = 1/(1 \times 0)$ is then infinite, so the standard
error becomes `NaN` and the confidence interval `NA`; $\hat S(3) = 0$. `survfit` reports
exactly the same thing (`std.err = NaN`, CI `NA` at time 3).

```{r}
time <- c(2, 2, 1, 3, 2)
status <- c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0)

knitr::kable(km_ci(time, status), digits = 3)
summary(survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, conf.type = "plain"))
```

The reason is that Greenwood's variance treats each event time like a binomial proportion
$d/n$; when *everyone* left in the risk set dies ($d = n$), there is no remaining
information with which to estimate the variance - the curve is forced down to 0 and its
uncertainty is undefined. This is a reminder that the plain Wald interval on $S$ is
unstable near the extremes, which is why transformed intervals (log or log-log) are used
in practice.
:::

# Kaplan-Meier plot

Create a simple plot function:

```{r}
plot_km <- function(x) ggplot(x, aes(time, S)) + geom_step()
```

Compare `plot_km(km(time, status))` and `plot(survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1), conf.int = FALSE)`.

**6.** How and why do the results differ (if they do)?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** 

- `plot_km(km(time, status))` starts at the first event time ($t = 2$, $S = 0.8$); it has
  no flat segment at $S = 1$ from time 0 to the first event.
- It does not extend to the last observation time (8).

```{r}
time <- c(2, 3, 5, 6, 8) # re-set to the original example data
status <- c(1, 1, 0, 1, 0)

plot_km(km(time, status))
plot(survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1), conf.int = FALSE)
```
:::

**7.** Explain (in words) how you would improve your functions (`km()`, `plot_km()` or both) to make your plot look like a real Kaplan-Meier plot.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** To make the plot look like a proper Kaplan-Meier plot you would:

- add a point $(0, 1)$ so the curve starts at 1 and is flat until the first event;
- extend the step to the largest observed (possibly censored) time;
:::

**Bonus:** Implement your suggested changes from (7) and check the result.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** One implementation (base `ggplot2` only):

```{r}
km3 <- function(time, status) {
  t <- sort(unique(time[status == 1]))
  n <- sapply(t, function(z) sum(time >= z))
  d <- sapply(t, function(z) sum(time == z & status == 1))
  data.frame(
    time = c(0, t),
    n = c(length(time), n),
    d = c(0, d),
    S = c(1, cumprod(1 - d / n))
  )
}

plot_km(km3(time, status)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1), xlim = c(0, max(time)))
```

(In practice the cleanest route is `ggsurvfit::ggsurvfit(survfit(...))`, which produces a
fully annotated plot automatically.)
:::

# Cox

Here is a simple Cox function for one covariate `x`:

```{r}
cox <- function(time, status, x, beta = 0, tol = 1) {
  repeat {
    U <- I <- 0 # score and information
    for (i in which(status == 1)) {
      R <- which(time >= time[i]) # Risk set
      w <- exp(beta * x[R])
      mean_x <- sum(w * x[R]) / sum(w)
      mean_x2 <- sum(w * x[R]^2) / sum(w)
      U <- U + x[i] - mean_x # Score
      I <- I + mean_x2 - mean_x^2 # Information
    }
    beta_new <- beta + U / I # Newton-Raphson
    if (abs(beta_new - beta) < tol) {
      break
    }
    beta <- beta_new
  }

  c(beta = beta_new, SE = sqrt(1 / I))
}
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Recapture section 3.3 from the book.
:::

**8.** As for `km()` (`km2()`), include the function definition above (copy and paste into a code block in your report) and add a  description of the function and comments within the function to explain what it does in more details.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** The function maximises the *partial likelihood* of a Cox proportional
hazards model with a single covariate `x`, using the Newton-Raphson algorithm. `U` is the
score (first derivative of the partial log-likelihood), `I` the observed information
(second derivative), and the estimate is updated by $\beta_{\text{new}} = \beta + U/I$;
at convergence the standard error is $\mathrm{SE} = 1/\sqrt I$.

```{r}
#| eval: false
cox <- function(time, status, x, beta = 0, tol = 1) {
  # Newton-Raphson iterations:
  # repeatedly update beta until the change in beta is sufficiently small
  repeat {
    # U(beta) = score = first derivative of the partial log-likelihood
    # I(beta) = observed information = - second derivative of the
    # partial log-likelihood
    #
    # Both are recomputed at the current value of beta in each iteration.
    U <- I <- 0

    # Loop over individuals who experience the event.
    #
    # If several individuals have an event at the same time, each contributes
    # separately but uses the SAME risk set. This corresponds to Breslow's
    # handling of tied event times.
    for (i in which(status == 1)) {
      # Risk set R_i:
      # all individuals still under observation and at risk immediately
      # before the event time of individual i.
      R <- which(time >= time[i])

      # Relative hazard for each individual in the risk set:
      #
      #     exp(beta * x_j)
      #
      # These are the weights appearing in the denominator of the
      # Cox partial likelihood.
      w <- exp(beta * x[R])

      # Risk-set weighted mean of x:
      #
      #       sum x_j exp(beta*x_j)
      # E(x) = ---------------------
      #         sum exp(beta*x_j)
      #
      # This is the expected value of x among individuals in the risk set,
      # weighted according to their current relative hazards.
      mean_x <- sum(w * x[R]) / sum(w)

      # Corresponding risk-set weighted mean of x^2.
      mean_x2 <- sum(w * x[R]^2) / sum(w)

      # Contribution to the score:
      #
      #     observed x for the individual with the event
      #                   -
      #     weighted expected x in the risk set
      #
      # Summing these contributions gives U(beta).
      # The MLE is the beta for which U(beta) = 0.
      U <- U + x[i] - mean_x

      # Contribution to the observed information:
      #
      #     E(x^2) - E(x)^2
      #
      # i.e. the weighted variance of x within the risk set.
      #
      # This is -d^2 l(beta)/d beta^2 for this event contribution.
      I <- I + mean_x2 - mean_x^2
    }

    # Newton-Raphson update.
    #
    # In general:
    #
    #   beta_new = beta - score / second derivative
    #
    # Since I = - second derivative here, this becomes
    #
    #   beta_new = beta + U / I
    #
    # Thus we move beta toward the value where the score U(beta) = 0.
    beta_new <- beta + U / I

    # Convergence criterion:
    # stop when the Newton-Raphson update changes beta by less than tol.
    if (abs(beta_new - beta) < tol) {
      break
    }

    # Use the updated estimate as the starting value for the next iteration.
    beta <- beta_new
  }

  # At convergence:
  #
  # beta_new is the maximum partial-likelihood estimate of beta.
  #
  # The approximate variance follows from the curvature of the
  # partial log-likelihood:
  #
  #     Var(beta_hat) ≈ 1 / I(beta_hat)
  #
  # and hence
  #
  #     SE(beta_hat) ≈ sqrt(1 / I(beta_hat)).
  c(
    beta = beta_new,
    SE = sqrt(1 / I)
  )
}
```
:::

Define a covariate `x <- c(0, 1, 0, 1, 1)`.

**9.** Compare `cox(time, status, x)` to the equivalent analysis performed by functions from the survival package.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** With the default `tol = 1`, `cox(time, status, x)` returns
$\hat\beta \approx -0.819$ and $\mathrm{SE} \approx 1.529$, whereas `coxph` returns
$\hat\beta = -0.752$ with $\mathrm{SE} = 1.436$ - the two do not agree.

```{r}
time <- c(2, 3, 5, 6, 8) # re-set to the original example data
status <- c(1, 1, 0, 1, 0)
x <- c(0, 1, 0, 1, 1)

cox(time, status, x)
coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ x)
```
:::

**10.** Do the results differ? If so, why? HINT: what is the purpose of argument `tol` (you may find `?coxph.control` relevant)? Try different values of `tol` and check if the results from `cox()` and `coxph()` can reach agreement.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** They differ because of the loose convergence tolerance. With `tol = 1` the
Newton-Raphson loop stops as soon as $|\beta_{\text{new}} - \beta| < 1$. Starting at
$\beta = 0$, the first update is $\beta_{\text{new}} = U/I \approx -0.819$, and since
$|{-0.819} - 0| < 1$ the loop breaks after a single step, returning an estimate that has
not converged to the maximum of the partial likelihood (and a standard error evaluated at
the wrong point). `coxph` instead iterates to convergence using a much tighter criterion
(see `?coxph.control`; the default `eps = 1e-9`) based on the log-likelihood.

The purpose of `tol` is precisely the convergence tolerance of the Newton-Raphson update.
Setting it small makes the two agree:

```{r}
cox(time, status, x, tol = 1e-8)
```
:::

# Analysis

We will use the `lung` data from the survival package. Read about it: `?lung`.

Try `with(lung, cox(time, status - 1, ph.karno))`.

**11.** Formulate a research question associated with the analysis (the code you tried).

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** For example: *"Is a patient's Karnofsky performance score at diagnosis
(`ph.karno`) associated with survival in the North Central Cancer Treatment Group (NCCTG)
lung cancer cohort, and how much does the hazard of death change per unit increase of the
score?"* Equivalently: does better baseline performance status predict longer survival?
:::

**12.** Did you get any result? If not, why? HINT: perform the same analysis with the equivalent survival package function and read the output carefully

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** No - `cox()` errors with `missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed`, because
`ph.karno` contains a missing value (the `lung` data has 228 rows and one `NA` in
`ph.karno`). The `NA` propagates through the weighted means into the score and
information, so `beta_new` becomes `NA` and `abs(NA - beta) < tol` cannot be evaluated.
`coxph` handles this by dropping incomplete cases: it reports `n = 227, number of events =
164 (1 observation deleted due to missingness)` - that line is the clue.

```{r}
try(with(lung, cox(time, status - 1, ph.karno)))
coxph(Surv(time, status - 1) ~ ph.karno, data = lung)
```
:::

**13.** Fix the problem and check that the result from `cox()` is equivalent to the result from the equivalent survival package function.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** Remove the incomplete case before calling `cox()`, and (per question 10) use
a tight tolerance:

```{r}
cc <- lung[complete.cases(lung$ph.karno), ]

cox(cc$time, cc$status - 1, cc$ph.karno, tol = 1e-8)
coxph(Surv(time, status - 1) ~ ph.karno, data = cc)
```

The two now agree (to within the numerical tolerance).
:::

**14.** Interpret the result and summarise your findings (using statistical, as well as clinical language).

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** The estimated log hazard ratio is $-0.0164$ (SE $0.0059$), so the hazard
ratio per one-point increase in Karnofsky score is $\exp(-0.0164) \approx 0.984$ with 95%
CI $(0.972,\,0.995)$; $z = -2.81$, $p = 0.005$.

```{r}
cc <- lung[complete.cases(lung$ph.karno), ]
m0 <- coxph(Surv(time, status - 1) ~ ph.karno, data = cc)

exp(coef(m0)) # hazard ratio
exp(confint(m0)) # 95% CI for the hazard ratio
exp(10 * coef(m0)) # hazard ratio for a 10-point difference
```

*Statistically:* the confidence interval excludes 1, so there is strong evidence of an
association - a higher Karnofsky score is associated with a lower hazard of death.

*Clinically:* each additional point of performance status is associated with about a
$1.6\%$ lower hazard. Over a 10-point difference this compounds to about a 15% lower
hazard for a patient scored 10 points higher. Patients in better functional condition at
diagnosis survive longer.
:::

**15.** How would you improve the analysis? You may reformulate the research question and you may use any available tool (methods/packages) for the analysis.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** Several improvements are possible:

- **Adjust for confounders.** The univariate model ignores other prognostic variables;
  fit a multivariable model (e.g. add `age` and `sex`).
- **Do not double-count performance status.** `ph.karno` and `ph.ecog` measure the same
  underlying construct (their correlation is about $-0.81$); include only one of them.
- **Check the functional form.** The model assumes the log hazard is *linear* in
  `ph.karno`; consider treating it as categorical or checking linearity.
- **Handle missing data deliberately.** Complete-case analysis drops one row; multiple
  imputation would use all observations.
- **Check the proportional-hazards assumption.** `cox.zph()` suggests `ph.karno` violates
  proportional hazards, i.e. its effect may weaken over time, so the single hazard ratio
  is a time-average.
:::

**16.** Perform your suggested analysis and present your results with relevant figures, tables and/or summaries/interpretations.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.** A multivariable model adjusting for age and sex:

```{r}
fit <- coxph(Surv(time, status - 1) ~ ph.karno + age + sex, data = lung)
gtsummary::tbl_regression(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)
modelsummary::modelsummary(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)
cox.zph(fit)
```

After adjusting for age and sex, the association of `ph.karno` persists but decrease in size. Being male roughly doubles the hazard relative to female (HR 0.608), while age is not clearly associated.

A caveat: `cox.zph(fit)` indicates `ph.karno` may violate proportional hazards, so these
hazard ratios should be read as time-averaged effects. A fuller analysis would also plot a
Kaplan-Meier curve stratified by performance-status groups and report the
proportional-hazards diagnostics.
:::
